title: Merit and giving
hookLine: at first light, monks walk past with bowls, and lay people fill them

lines: FIRST LIGHT. A LINE OF BOWLS.
cards: First light on a street in a Theravada town. A line of monks walks barefoot, in single file, each holding a covered bowl against the belly.
At the curb, people are already waiting: a grandmother with a pot of steaming rice, a kid with a bag of fruit, a man on his way to work with a packet of sticky rice. The monks stop. Lids come off.
Spoonfuls go in. Nobody haggles. Nobody pays.
The monks don't ask for anything, and in the custom of the round they receive the food quietly and walk on. The odd part, to an outside eye, is who seems grateful. It's the people at the curb.

teach.h: THE BOWL IS A REAL NEED.
teach.b: Dana is the Pali and Sanskrit word for giving. First, the bowl is a real need. Under the monk's rule, monks don't cook for themselves or store food, so the morning round is how they eat.
The texts describe a two-way bond: lay people give food, robes and shelter, and monks give the teaching. In one short discourse, the Buddha says the two groups support each other. Second, merit.

Buddhists speak of giving as making merit, a good that comes back to the giver and ripens over time. That's why the person at the curb can be the grateful one: the bowl is an open door, and the monk is holding it open.
In a discourse on a good gift, the Buddha describes the giver as glad before giving, bright in mind while giving, and content after. The gift isn't finished when the rice leaves the spoon.

teach.h: FOOD, TIME, A WORD: ALL DANA.
teach.b: Fourth, dana isn't only food for monks. Teachers in this tradition talk about giving time, attention, a meal to a neighbor, a kind word.

And in the Dhammapada, the Buddha says the gift of the teaching surpasses every other gift. A bowl of rice and a good word belong to the same practice, and neither needs a monk walking past your door.

how: In Theravada countries, lay Buddhists often place food in monks' bowls on the morning alms round or bring meals to the monastery, and speak of this giving as making merit.

o: a yearly temple tax paid by each household
giving freely, which gladdens the one who gives
a fee monks charge for a blessing or teaching

s: on the alms round, monks ask for the food they want
the monks don't ask. people give, and the monks receive quietly.
Buddhists speak of giving as making merit for the giver
a good that comes back to the giver, which is why the giver can be the grateful one.
in the Dhammapada, the gift of the teaching is called the greatest gift
the Buddha says the gift of the teaching surpasses every other gift.

games.q: you're at the curb at first light. a monk stops, and you spoon rice into his bowl. what does he do, by the custom of the round?
o: thanks you warmly and offers a coin back.
asks for more rice for the monastery.
receives it quietly and walks on.
games.why: he receives it quietly and walks on. in the tradition's way of seeing it, the chance to give is itself the gift, so the giver is the grateful one.

practice: Bring to mind someone you'll see soon, a coworker, a neighbor, someone at home or on the street, and picture handing them something to eat: a coffee, half your lunch, a plate set down without being asked.
Stay with the before part, the gladness the discourse talks about, if it shows up. If it doesn't, just keep the person and the food in mind.

wordCard.voice: Dana. Giving: the food in the monk's bowl, and any gift offered freely, which the Buddha's teaching says gladdens the giver before, during and after. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali dāna: giving, generosity.

carryVoice: Your line: dana. The giver is glad before, bright during, content after. See you tomorrow.
